concepts.def: Process by which information from a gene leads to a functional product (protein or RNA).
Protein that binds to DNA, switching genes on or off by promoting or blocking RNA polymerase.
Heritable changes in gene expression without altering DNA base sequence, via DNA methylation and histone modification.

Mutated proto-oncogene whose product drives uncontrolled cell division, contributing to tumour formation.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Control of Gene Expression — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Control of Gene Expression brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Control of Gene Expression.

mcqs.q: Stem cells able to form all body cell types but not extra-embryonic tissue are:
options: Totipotent
Pluripotent
Multipotent
Unipotent

mcqs.q: What does a gene code for?
options: Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
A gene codes for a specific physical feature like eye colour directly.
Typically a polypeptide (protein) — through transcription to mRNA and translation by ribosomes.
Insulin works on muscles and glucagon works on the brain.

mcqs.q: Why is negative feedback the default mechanism in homeostasis?
options: Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
It opposes deviations from a set point, returning the variable toward its normal value — keeping internal conditions stable.
Negative feedback only operates when something goes wrong in the body.
Negative feedback amplifies changes to make them more noticeable.

mcqs.q: How do insulin and glucagon work together to regulate blood glucose?
options: They are antagonistic — insulin lowers blood glucose (cells take up glucose, store as glycogen); glucagon raises it (glycogen broken back down to glucose).
Insulin and glucagon both lower blood glucose using different mechanisms.
Insulin works on muscles and glucagon works on the brain.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
